patches.old: For the MCAT, memorize the rough correspondence: every ~5.7 kJ/mol change in ΔG°′ at 37°C shifts the equilibrium by approximately one order of magnitude. A ΔG°′ of −17 kJ/mol corresponds to a Keq of roughly 1000.
patches.new: For the MCAT, memorize the rough correspondence: at 37 °C, every ~5.9 kJ/mol change in ΔG°′ shifts the equilibrium by about one order of magnitude (it is 5.7 at 25 °C, which is the figure most general chemistry courses quote). A ΔG°′ of −18 kJ/mol therefore corresponds to a Keq near 1000.
patches.reason: The constant quoted is the 25 °C value. RT ln 10 is 5.71 kJ/mol at 298 K but 5.93 kJ/mol at 310 K, and the sentence specifies 37 °C. The worked figure was wrong for the same reason: at 37 °C a ΔG°′ of −17 kJ/mol gives Keq ≈ 740, not 1000; −18 kJ/mol gives ≈ 1000. Both corrected, with the 25 °C value kept in parentheses since students meet both.

patches.old: For palmitate (16 carbons), 7 cycles of beta-oxidation plus oxidation of 8 acetyl-CoA units yields approximately 106 ATP, minus the 2 ATP equivalents for activation = **net ~104 ATP per palmitate**.
patches.new: For palmitate (16 carbons), 7 cycles of beta-oxidation give 7 FADH₂ (~10.5 ATP) and 7 NADH (~17.5 ATP), and the 8 acetyl-CoA units yield ~80 ATP — about 108 gross. Subtracting the 2 ATP equivalents spent on activation gives **net ~106 ATP per palmitate**.
patches.reason: The arithmetic was off by two. Using the P/O ratios this lesson itself adopts (NADH ≈ 2.5, FADH₂ ≈ 1.5, acetyl-CoA ≈ 10), palmitate gives 10.5 + 17.5 + 80 = 108 gross and 106 net, which is the figure current textbooks quote. The lesson had 106 gross and 104 net. The working is now shown so the number can be reconstructed rather than memorised.

patches.old: But ATP cannot phosphorylate ADP to make PEP—that would require an even more favorable driving reaction.
patches.new: But ATP cannot phosphorylate pyruvate to make PEP — that runs up the ladder, and would need a more powerful donor than ATP. (This is exactly why gluconeogenesis cannot simply reverse pyruvate kinase, and has to spend two high-energy bonds going round through oxaloacetate instead.)
patches.reason: "ATP cannot phosphorylate ADP to make PEP" names the wrong substrate: phosphorylating ADP yields ATP, not PEP. The reaction meant is pyruvate → PEP. Corrected, and tied to the gluconeogenesis bypass the lesson describes two sections later, which is the reason this fact is tested.

sources.title: Berg, Tymoczko & Stryer, Biochemistry — phosphoryl transfer potential
sources.note: ΔG°′ of hydrolysis (kJ/mol): PEP −61.9, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate −49.3, creatine phosphate −43.1, ATP→ADP+Pi −30.5, AMP −14.2, glucose-6-phosphate −13.8. Phosphoryl groups transfer from higher to lower potential.

sources.title: Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry — ATP yield from fatty acid oxidation
sources.note: Palmitate: 7 rounds of β-oxidation give 7 FADH₂ and 7 NADH plus 8 acetyl-CoA; with P/O ratios of 1.5 and 2.5 and 10 ATP per acetyl-CoA this is 108 gross, less 2 ATP equivalents for activation, giving ~106 net.

visual.title: The phosphoryl transfer ladder
visual.alt: A vertical ladder of phosphorylated compounds ranked by the standard free energy of hydrolysis, from phosphoenolpyruvate at −61.9 kJ/mol down to glucose-6-phosphate at −13.8, with ATP highlighted at −30.5 in the middle and an arrow showing that phosphoryl groups transfer downward. Beside it, worked arithmetic for pyruvate kinase recharging ATP (net −31.4) and hexokinase spending it (net −16.7), with panels on the shared-intermediate requirement for coupling and on the ATP-to-AMP route that spends two high-energy bonds.
visual.caption: ATP's position in the middle is the whole point: everything above can recharge it, and it can pay everything below. A currency has to be able to take payment as well as make it.
